US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth attends a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia, on November 11, 2026 [AFP]By Hoda SherifPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
In the wake of the United States midterm elections, attention has turned to whether Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will be able to preserve his cabinet-level position once Congress’s new Democratic majorities are sworn in.
Already, the Fox News host-turned-military-chief has faced mounting calls for his removal from office.

But analysts question the extent to which Hegseth’s impeachment would affect military policy under President Donald Trump.
“Ultimately, the secretary of defence is a powerful participant in shaping a war,” said Jasmine El-Gamal, a former Middle East adviser in the Pentagon.
El-Gamal, however, believes targeting Hegseth alone would not be enough to secure accountability for decisions like launching the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hegseth holds significant power in directing the US war effort, she explained, but he also works hand-in-hand with the president and his advisers.
“Calling him merely an ‘executor’ understates that power, while calling him its sole architect understates the president’s power and obscures where particular decisions were actually made,” El-Gamal said.

People fill jerrycans with drinking water from a charity tank in the southwestern city of Taiz, Yemen [File: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters]By AbdulHakim HelalPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
Taiz, Yemen – Qaid al-Sharaabi waited three days before it was his turn to receive a tanker of clean water.
But the delay is not the only problem. He says he now has to pay more – the result of the Houthi siege on Taiz, in southwestern Yemen.

“This is the second time since the siege began a month-and-a-half ago that I’ve had to pay twice the price for a water tanker,” al-Sharaabi told Al Jazeera. “I’m afraid that if things continue like this, more residents will resort to using unsafe water.”
The United Nations children’s agency (UNICEF) says that water production in Taiz has nearly halved, while more than 800,000 people are reported to be cut off from humanitarian assistance.
The crisis has left the city reeling, even as government soldiers try to defend it, in the latest round of fighting to hit the area since the war in Yemen started in 2014.
Hospital administrators are warning of a public health disaster, while government officials are unsure how much longer they will have the funds needed to carry out even limited services.
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, has long suffered from severe water shortages.

Anthropic, the maker of Claude, is now trading on the Nasdaq through the largest initial public offering in history, surpassing the debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
The stock began trading on the ticker ANT midday on Thursday.

By the time the stock ultimately went live, at 11:50am in New York (16:50 GMT), it was trading at $111.50 per share, a 34 percent rise.

Tim Jones voted for Brexit but as a business owner, has been disappointed with the realities of leaving the EU [Al Jazeera]By Rory ChallandsPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
Lincolnshire, United Kingdom – A decade is a short time in cheesemaking. Barrels of Tim Jones’ “Lincolnshire Poachers” cheese rest on their racks for months and years, disturbed only by Florence, the robot cheese turner.
Complexity, depth and flavour develop with patience.

The most mature cheese in Tim’s Lincolnshire dairy, in the English midlands, is five years old. By that measure, it was only a couple of cheeses ago that 52 percent of the British public voted for the country’s most tumultuous constitutional revolt in living memory.
Jones was one of them. But he is under no illusion that it went well – particularly for his exports.
“It suddenly made life much harder. We lost certain customers, and it became more expensive to get the cheese there. It definitely harmed our business,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ten years after the UK voted to leave the European Union, few are happy with what they got.Jones, a Brexit voter, has some regrets about his decision [Al Jazeera]

Bilal Erdogan, centre, greets his Lebanese supporters who welcome him in Tripoli, northern Lebanon, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026 [AP Photo]
Some journeys feel less like a first visit and more like a homecoming. That is how I felt during my three days in Lebanon — my first ever visit to a country I had long known through its history, its poets and its people, but had never walked through myself.
I came at the kind invitation of Dr Tarek Mitri, Deputy Prime Minister of Lebanon, who proved the most gracious of hosts. I came in a spirit of friendship and partnership, and I leave with gratitude. In every conversation — in Beirut, in Tripoli, in Akkar and beyond — I heard the same quiet determination: Lebanon wants to stand on its own feet, and it wants partners, not patrons.
I also leave with a full heart and, I must admit, a fuller stomach. From a za’atar breakfast on the road to Akkar to the sweets of Hallab in Tripoli and shawarma at Barbar in Beirut, Lebanese hospitality is everything people promise. Around shared tables, over strong coffee and long conversations, I was reminded that the bonds between our peoples were never only about diplomacy. Distance on a map tells you very little. What matters is the geography of hearts — and by that measure, Beirut and Istanbul have always been neighbours.
That warmth carries a responsibility, for friendship is proved not in words but in what we do together. Five convictions stayed with me throughout the visit.
1. Unity is Lebanon’s greatest strength
Lebanon’s diversity of faiths, communities and traditions is not a weakness to be managed; it is a richness to be protected. I was honoured to...

Rohingya refugees hold placards ahead of the International Court of Justice verdict in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingya population, at a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, November 19, 2026 [Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters]By Shola LawalPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya minority ethnic group.
After seven years of deliberations, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa delivered the long-awaited ruling on Thursday in a verdict which took three hours to read out.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4UN’s top court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingyalist 2 of 4‘We want to go back’: Rohingya refugees pin hopes on ICJ genocide verdictlist 3 of 4ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingyalist 4 of 4ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case: What to expectend of list
Nine of the 15-judge panel found that Myanmar has committed genocide, the court said. Justices also voted in favour of a landmark reparations order against the country which it says has persecuted the mostly Muslim group for decades.
It is the first time in the history of the World Court, which was established in 1945, that it has ruled that a state has committed genocide. The decision is final and cannot be appealed.
The Gambia brought the landmark case against Myanmar in 2019.
After many years of persecution, Myanmar’s military launched an offensive in 2017 which forced about 750,000 Rohingya from their homes and lands, and pushed them into squalid refugee camps, largely in neighbouring Bangladesh.
About 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the early stages of the military operation. Thousands of others died in shipwrecks as the...

item.description:

play video

What happens when Israeli soldiers return from Gaza?
The film ‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide examines the psychological consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza through personal accounts of injury, grief and trauma by Israeli soldiers, alongside interviews with psychologists, journalists and Palestinian trauma specialists.
The film looks at the violence inflicted on Palestinians and asks how its consequences reach into Israeli families and society. Soldiers’ accounts of sleeplessness and fear sit alongside questions about military mental healthcare and the lasting effects of prolonged war.
Watch ‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide, part of Cost of War, from Al Jazeera Originals.Published On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
